stops.name: Denver: the birth in the engineer's house
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'John Searle (philosopher)'; Britannica; American Philosophical Association In Memoriam). The parents' occupations are attested in the same sources. stops.campa: G. W. Searle is an electrical engineer at AT&T; Hester Beck Searle is a physician. Their son John Rogers Searle is born in Denver on the last day of July 1932, into a house kept by a man who tests whether a circuit carries current and a woman who tests whether a diagnosis is right. The record of the birth gives the date and the two professions and then stops. No street, no hospital, no note of how long the family stays in Colorado. The obituaries written ninety-three years later begin from the same two professions.

stops.name: Bascom Hall, Madison: the undergraduate
stops.date_confidence: the Wisconsin years are given in the pool as roughly 1949 to 1952 with no matriculation date; the year is the pool's earliest bound and the month and day default to 01. stops.campa: He enrolls at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, reading philosophy and economics, and climbs Bascom Hill to lectures in a state whose junior senator is at that moment the most feared man in American public life. Searle is not yet twenty. He reads there for three years and takes no degree from the place: the record puts him at Madison from about 1949 to 1952 and then gone, out of the country on a scholarship, with the American degree unfinished and never afterwards completed.

stops.name: Memorial Union, Madison: Students Against Joseph McCarthy
stops.date_confidence: year attested only loosely: Wikipedia dates the activism to 1950 and gives Searle's role as secretary of Students Against Joseph McCarthy, while the Grokipedia biography and the Reason interview add that he was president of the Wisconsin Student Association. The two offices are not incompatible but no single source carries both, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than resolved. stops.campa: He serves as secretary of Students Against Joseph McCarthy and, by one account, as president of the Wisconsin Student Association, organizing against the senator inside the senator's own state while the hearings are running. It is his first schooling in what an utterance does when an institution stands behind it: a name read aloud in a committee room ends a career with no court sitting anywhere. Nothing he publishes for the next twenty years mentions McCarthy. Which of the two offices he actually held, no surviving account settles.

stops.name: Madison: the Rhodes Scholarship in the junior year
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'John Searle (philosopher)'), which places the award in his junior year; month and day default to 01. stops.campa: In his junior year he wins a Rhodes Scholarship. He is nineteen, has not finished his American degree, and will not go back to finish it. The scholarship carries him to Oxford for seven years and three degrees, into the one philosophy faculty then arguing that the way to settle an old problem is to look at how ordinary people actually use the words in it, and that a philosopher who ignores what a man would actually say is arguing about nothing. What the selection committee saw in him, and what he said to them, is not recorded anywhere.

stops.name: Christ Church, Oxford: the Rhodes scholar comes up
stops.date_confidence: the year 1952 and the college are attested (Wikipedia; Justapedia); the Michaelmas term arrival is inferred from ordinary Oxford practice and the month is not documented in the pool. The day defaults to 01. Coordinate is the pool's Christ Church pin, 51.7500/-1.2558.
stops.campa: Searle comes up to Christ Church on the Rhodes money, the largest and grandest of the Oxford colleges. The philosophy schools here are dominated by a method that treats the ordinary use of words as evidence rather than as noise: what would a man actually say, and when, and what follows once he has said it. He takes his BA in 1955 and stays on. The American who arrived arguing about a senator learns to argue about whether the words I promise report an inner act or perform an outward one.

stops.name: All Souls College, Oxford: the Saturday Mornings
stops.date_confidence: contradiction recorded, not resolved. The geography lens of this file's pool places Austin's informal Saturday Mornings group at Magdalen College and tags the venue as reconstruction; that college is wrong for Searle's years in any case, since Austin held the Magdalen fellowship from 1935 but was White's Professor of Moral Philosophy and a Professorial Fellow of Corpus Christi College from 1952 onward, which spans the whole of Searle's Oxford period. j_l_austin.journey.json fixes the group at All Souls from 1947, following EBSCO Research Starters, and uses the coordinate 51.7526/-1.2529; that canonical pin is inherited here, with the Magdalen and Corpus Christi alternatives recorded. Searle's own attendance is standard in accounts of Austin's circle but is not documented to any dated meeting; the year is an ordering device and month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: On Saturday mornings a small group of dons meets to take a philosophical problem apart word by word under the direction of J. L. Austin, White's Professor of Moral Philosophy. Grice, Strawson, Hart and Warnock pass through it. Austin is working out, in front of them, the class of utterances that describe nothing and do something: I name this ship, I bet you sixpence, I do. Searle sits in the room where speech act theory is assembled out of examples, years before any of it is a book. Austin will publish almost none of it alive.
suggested_refs: j_l_austin.journey.json, 'All Souls College, Oxford, the Saturday Mornings begin'

stops.name: University College, Oxford: reading with Strawson
stops.date_confidence: the supervision by Strawson alongside Austin is attested (Wikipedia; Barry Smith, 'John Searle: From Speech Acts to Social Reality'). The pool's University College coordinate, 51.7513/-1.2494, sits on the High Street frontage and is carried unchanged though it is close to the pin j_l_austin.journey.json uses for the Examination Schools; no better coordinate is in the pool. The year is an ordering device within the doctoral period and month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Searle has a second supervisor. Peter Strawson, at work on reference, on how a sentence picks out the thing it is about, takes him alongside Austin. The doctoral subject sits exactly between the two men: the problems that arise in a theory of meaning out of the notions of sense and reference. Austin gives him the act, the thing an utterance does. Strawson gives him the aboutness, the thing an utterance is directed at. Of the supervisions themselves nothing survives: no notes, no correspondence, no record of what either man told him to cut.
suggested_refs: P. F. Strawson, 'On Referring' (1950), the paper behind the supervision
sources: Barry Smith, 'John Searle: From Speech Acts to Social Reality'

stops.name: Christ Church, Oxford: lecturer at twenty-four
stops.date_confidence: the Christ Church lectureship, 1956 to 1959, is attested in the Justapedia biography and repeated in the Barry Smith account; month and day default to 01. No teaching record, lecture list, or salary is in the pool.
stops.campa: Before the doctorate is finished Searle is made a lecturer in philosophy at Christ Church, teaching in the college he entered as a scholarship student four years earlier. He is twenty-four. For three years he holds an Oxford teaching post and an unfinished thesis at the same time, and the two run out together in 1959, the lectureship ending in the year the doctorate is examined. He is teaching the philosophy of language inside a college he had entered four years earlier as a foreign scholarship student. The lecture lists for those three years have not survived.

stops.name: Oxford: the thesis on sense and reference
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, which gives the full title 'Problems arising in the theory of meaning out of the notions of sense and reference'); month and day default to 01. The pin is the city, since the pool does not name an examination venue. The pool's afterlife lens gives an Oxford coordinate of 51.7548/-1.2544; the canonical city pin from j_l_austin.journey.json, 51.7520/-1.2577, is used instead.
stops.campa: The thesis is finished and submitted: Problems arising in the theory of meaning out of the notions of sense and reference. It is examined at Oxford, supervised by Austin and Strawson, and it is never published as a book. Its work goes instead into a set of conditions Searle spends the next ten years hardening into rules, the conditions under which saying a thing counts as promising it, asserting it, ordering it, naming it. Seven years after arriving on a scholarship he leaves England with three degrees and a job in California.

stops.name: Berkeley: the appointment he never leaves
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia; Britannica; APA In Memoriam); the September start is inferred from the American academic calendar and is not documented, and the day defaults to 01. The coordinate is inherited byte-identical from j_l_austin.journey.json's Berkeley stop, 37.8703/-122.2593, a representative campus pin at Wheeler Hall; the pool's own Berkeley pins vary between 37.8695 and 37.8719. The pool's phrase 'a career of exactly sixty years at the same institution' is a constructed figure and is not used: it counts the 2019 disciplinary action as the terminus of the career, when Searle had stopped active teaching well before it, and his association with Berkeley ran from 1959 to his death in 2025, sixty-six years.
stops.campa: Searle joins the philosophy department at the University of California, Berkeley, and does not leave it. His own supervisor had lectured on this campus the previous autumn, arguing against sense-data in front of a Berkeley audience: J. L. Austin came west in 1958, and the student arrives in 1959 and holds no other post for the rest of his life. The department is building itself into one of the strongest in the country. Searle is twenty-seven. The theory of speech acts he brings west with him will not be a book for another ten years.
suggested_refs: j_l_austin.journey.json, 'Berkeley, the case against sense-data' (September 1958)

stops.name: Sproul Plaza: the first tenured man to cross
stops.date_confidence: the year and Searle's status as the first tenured professor to join the Free Speech Movement are attested (Wikipedia; Berkeley News archive; Free Speech Movement histories). The December rally in front of Sproul Hall and the presence of Mario Savio on the same steps come from the pool's geography lens; the day is not recorded and defaults to 01.
stops.campa: In December, with the campus shut down and the administration facing a student strike, Searle addresses a rally in front of Sproul Hall, the first tenured professor to take the students' side in public. Mario Savio speaks from the same steps. The Free Speech Movement is a quarrel about precisely the thing Searle studies for a living: which utterances an institution may forbid, in which places, and what it means for a university to license speech at all. He is thirty-two and he is standing on the plaza.
suggested_refs: Free Speech Movement Digital Archive, UC Berkeley, Sproul Hall footage of December 1964

stops.name: Berkeley: special assistant to the chancellor
stops.date_confidence: the post and the break with the movement's radical wing are attested to roughly 1965-1967 in the pool's geography lens, following Berkeley News and Free Speech Movement histories; no appointment date is given and month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: The movement turns, and Searle turns with it. He breaks with the radical wing and takes a post as special assistant to the chancellor for student affairs, working inside the administration he had confronted from the steps a few months before. Colleagues who cheered him in December are calling him a defector by spring. He is not persuadable by either camp: the man who insists that a promise binds the speaker also insists that a university's rules bind the students who study under them. He holds the post two years.
suggested_refs: UC Berkeley chancellor's office records, 1965-1967

stops.name: Berkeley: the Academic Freedom Committee in the year of People's Park
stops.date_confidence: the chairmanship of the Academic Freedom Committee during the People's Park dispute is attested to 1969 (Wikipedia, 'John Searle (philosopher)'); no month is given and month and day default to 01. Nothing in the pool records what the committee decided or published that year, and that is a gap.
stops.campa: Berkeley in 1969 is a city under a state of emergency: the fight over People's Park brings the National Guard into the streets and helicopters over the campus. Searle chairs the Academic Freedom Committee through it, the body that has to rule on what a professor and a student may say and where they may say it. Five years earlier he had stood on the other side of the same question, on the plaza, in front of Sproul. What the committee concluded in that year of guardsmen and tear gas does not survive in anything written about him since.

segments.name: Speech Acts, and the Quarrel Over Iterability

stops.name: Cambridge: Speech Acts published
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'Speech Acts (book)'; Cambridge University Press publication record); month and day default to 01. Coordinate contradiction recorded: the pool's chronology lens gives Cambridge as 52.2053/0.1218 and its geography lens gives 52.2043/0.1149 for Cambridge University Press; the second is taken, matching the Cambridge pin already in alan_turing.journey.json. Neither is the press's Shaftesbury Road address.
stops.campa: Cambridge University Press publishes Speech Acts: An Essay in the Philosophy of Language. It takes Austin's lectures, which existed as notes and reached print only after his death, and hardens them into a system: to promise, to assert, to request is to perform an act governed by rules that can be written out, condition by condition. What was a set of examples in an Oxford common room is now a book with numbered conditions in it, and this is the form in which the theory will be taught, cited and attacked for the next fifty years. Searle is thirty-six, ten years into the Berkeley post, and this is his first book.
stops.quote: Human communication has some extraordinary properties, not shared by most other kinds of human behavior. One of the most extraordinary is this: If I am trying to tell someone something, then (assuming certain conditions are satisfied) as soon as he recognizes that I am trying to tell him something and exactly what it is I am trying to tell him, I have succeeded in telling it to him.
stops.quote_source: John Searle, Speech Acts: An Essay in the Philosophy of Language (Cambridge University Press, 1969), quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry 'Speech Acts'
suggested_refs: j_l_austin.journey.json, 'Clarendon Press, Oxford, How to Do Things with Words' (1962), the book this one systematizes

stops.name: Baltimore: Reiterating the Differences
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'Searle-Derrida debate'); month and day default to 01. Glyph was published by the Johns Hopkins University Press and the coordinate is the city of Baltimore, not a building. Searle himself is in Berkeley; the pin marks the place of publication, not the man. On the other side of the exchange: 'Signature Event Context' was first printed in Marges de la philosophie (Editions de Minuit, Paris, 1972), and was delivered before that as a conference paper at Montreal in August 1971, at the Congres international des Societes de philosophie de langue francaise. The pool's chronology lens gave its place only as 'France' with the geometric centroid of the country for a coordinate, which is discarded; the Montreal delivery is carried from the pool's own correction note, which flags it as wanting one further check.
stops.campa: Jacques Derrida has argued that Austin's theory cannot stand, because any utterance can be quoted, cited, written down, repeated in a play or a novel, and that this iterability is not a parasitic special case but the condition of language itself. Searle answers in the journal Glyph, out of Johns Hopkins, under the title Reiterating the Differences: Derrida has misread Austin, confused a type with its tokens, and taken a methodological exclusion for a metaphysical one. Searle is in Berkeley the whole time, and nothing in the record puts the two men in one room.
suggested_refs: Jacques Derrida, 'Signature Event Context' (1972), the essay being answered
j_l_austin.journey.json, 'Harvard University Press, Cambridge, the corrected second edition' (1975), which notes this reply as still to come

stops.name: Berkeley: Expression and Meaning
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'John Searle', bibliography). The pool splits on the pin: the chronology lens places the book at Cambridge University Press in England, the geography lens at UC Berkeley where it was written. The Berkeley pin is taken because the stop is Searle's, not the press's. The fiction essay collected here first appeared as 'The Logical Status of Fictional Discourse' in New Literary History, 1974-75. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Expression and Meaning collects ten years of refinement: a taxonomy of illocutionary acts, an account of indirect speech in which can you pass the salt asks a question and issues a request at once, a treatment of metaphor, and an essay on fiction. The novelist, Searle argues, performs assertions without asserting, pretending in a way the reader is in on, under conventions that suspend the ordinary commitment to truth. It is the machinery Austin built for a man saying I do, extended to a man writing a story about a man saying I do.
suggested_refs: John Searle, 'The Logical Status of Fictional Discourse', New Literary History (1974-75), collected in this volume

stops.campa: Speech Acts crosses into Spanish as Actos de habla: ensayo de filosofia del lenguaje, in Luis M. Valdes Villanueva's translation for Ediciones Catedra in Madrid, reprinted for the next thirty years; Planeta-Agostini reissues the same text in Barcelona in 1992 under licence. The book that began as Austin's unpublished Oxford notes is a set text in Spanish-language philosophy faculties on two continents, and the man who wrote it has nothing to do with the printings beyond the royalties. No Spanish edition carries a new preface by him.

stops.name: Evanston: the reply withheld from Limited Inc
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'Searle-Derrida debate'); month and day default to 01. The coordinate is Evanston, Illinois, the seat of Northwestern University Press, and again marks a publication rather than a place Searle went.
stops.campa: Derrida's rejoinder, and the whole exchange, is gathered by Northwestern University Press as Limited Inc. Searle refuses permission for his own reply to be reprinted inside it. The book therefore appears carrying Derrida's essays, Derrida's long answer to Searle, and a summary of what Searle had argued, but not Searle's own words. A philosopher who has spent twenty years explaining what an author does by putting a sentence into circulation declines, in this one case, to let his sentence circulate.

stops.name: Berkeley: the man with the rulebook
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'Chinese room'; Britannica, 'Minds, Brains, and Programs'); no composition date or place within Berkeley is documented and month and day default to 01. The coordinate is the canonical Berkeley pin inherited from j_l_austin.journey.json. Quote reallocated on the pool's own correction: the axiom 'Syntax is not by itself sufficient for, nor constitutive of, semantics' is real and verbatim but the Stanford Encyclopedia introduces it as Searle 1984, that is Minds, Brains and Science, not the 1980 paper the pool first attributed it to; it has been moved to the 1984 stop and this stop carries a sentence the same entry does attribute to the 1980 article.
stops.campa: Searle imagines a man locked in a room with a rulebook. Chinese characters come in through a slot; the man, who knows no Chinese, matches them against the rules and passes other characters back out. To everyone outside, the room answers in fluent Chinese. Inside, nobody understands a word of it. This is what a computer running a program is doing, Searle argues, and no amount of speed or complexity turns a rulebook into comprehension. The whole thing takes a page to set out. The man in the room never learns what any of it says, and never needs to.
stops.quote: The computer understanding is not just (like my understanding of German) partial or incomplete; it is zero.
stops.quote_source: John Searle, 'Minds, Brains, and Programs', Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3 (1980), quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Chinese Room Argument'
suggested_refs: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Chinese Room Argument'

stops.name: Cambridge: the target article and its commentaries
stops.date_confidence: the publication year and the journal are attested (Behavioral and Brain Sciences 3 (1980): 417-457; Britannica; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy). The month is an ordering device only and is not documented; the day defaults to 01. Superlative corrected: the pool called it the journal's most-commented target article in its history and sourced that to the Stanford Encyclopedia, which says no such thing. The Encyclopedia gives only the checkable figure, comments and criticisms by twenty-seven cognitive science researchers; the phrase 'most influential target article' is Wikipedia's, reporting the journal, and it is that weaker claim which is carried in the campa. stops.campa: Behavioral and Brain Sciences prints Minds, Brains, and Programs in its house format, with the commentaries of twenty-seven cognitive scientists attached, so the argument arrives already surrounded by objections and by Searle's answers to them. The systems reply, the robot reply, the brain simulator reply, the other minds reply, all are in the issue and all are answered in it. The journal will come to call it the most influential target article it has printed. Searle is arguing against Alan Turing's imitation game of 1950, the test that made behaviour the whole criterion of thinking.

stops.name: Berkeley: Intentionality
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'John Searle', bibliography; Cambridge University Press record). As with Expression and Meaning, the pool splits between the Cambridge press pin and the Berkeley pin; Berkeley is taken as the place of work. Month and day default to 01.
stops.campa: Intentionality: An Essay in the Philosophy of Mind supplies the other half of the argument. If syntax cannot produce meaning, something else must, and Searle's answer is that mental states are directed at the world in a way that is a biological fact about brains and not a formal property of any system that mimics them. A belief is about something; a desire is for something; and the aboutness is put there by a mind, not added by an observer reading the output. Cambridge University Press prints it in 1983, three years after the room.
suggested_refs: John Searle, Intentionality: An Essay in the Philosophy of Mind (Cambridge University Press, 1983)

The man in the room goes out over the radio to people who have never opened a philosophy journal and never will, and the claim that a machine can pass every behavioural test while understanding nothing enters ordinary conversation about computers a full generation before there are machines that pass such tests. Searle is fifty-one and speaking into a microphone in London.

stops.name: Moses Hall, Berkeley: teaching the room
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Searle's decades of Berkeley lecturing are general knowledge and the course recordings survive on the Internet Archive, but the pool's own geography lens marks the attribution of the lectures to Moses Hall, the philosophy department building, as reasonable inference rather than a sourced fact. The lectures are recorded and end up on the open web. Students who will go on to build the machines Searle says can understand nothing hear the objection first from him.

stops.name: Berkeley: the restatement
stops.date_confidence: the 1989 restatement is dated by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy entry from which the quotation is taken; month and day default to 01. The publication carrying it is not named in the pool, which is a gap.
stops.campa: Nine years of replies have not moved him. Searle restates the case in its barest form: formal symbols have no meaning at all except what something outside the system gives them, and a program is nothing but formal symbols. The room is not an argument about how hard the problem is, or how much computing power would be needed, or what a future machine might manage. It is an argument that a certain kind of thing is not the kind of thing that can mean anything, however well it performs. The objections keep arriving in the same four or five shapes.
stops.quote: Formal symbols by themselves can never be enough for mental contents, because the symbols, by definition, have no meaning (or interpretation, or semantics) except insofar as someone outside the system gives it to them.
stops.quote_source: John Searle, 1989 restatement of the Chinese Room argument, quoted in the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Chinese Room Argument'
suggested_refs: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Chinese Room Argument', section on the systems and robot replies
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'The Chinese Room Argument'

stops.name: Cambridge, Massachusetts: The Rediscovery of the Mind
stops.date_confidence: year and publisher attested (Wikipedia, 'John Searle', bibliography; MIT Press record); month and day default to 01. The coordinate is the pool's Cambridge, Massachusetts pin and is not the MIT Press address; j_l_austin.journey.json uses 42.3736/-71.1190 for Harvard University Press in the same city, and the two pins differ by about 700 metres.
stops.campa: The Rediscovery of the Mind goes after both sides of the standard quarrel at once: dualism, which makes the mind a second substance, and the materialisms that dispose of consciousness by denying that there is any. Searle's position is that consciousness is as real as digestion and, like digestion, is caused by biological processes in an organ. The dualists will not have it and the materialists will not have it, and the cognitive science of the decade is built on the computational theory he is attacking. MIT Press publishes it in 1992.
suggested_refs: John Searle, The Rediscovery of the Mind (MIT Press, 1992)

stops.name: New York: the twenty-dollar bill and the wedding
stops.date_confidence: year and publisher attested (Wikipedia, 'John Searle', bibliography; Free Press, New York). The coordinate is the city of publication; month and day default to 01. The pool's geography lens instead pins the book to Berkeley, where it was written, and the discrepancy is recorded.
stops.campa: The Construction of Social Reality turns the machinery outward. Money, marriage, borders, universities, a twenty-dollar bill: none of these is a physical fact and all of them are as hard as facts. They exist, Searle argues, because a formula is uttered by someone authorized to utter it and enough people go on accepting the result. I pronounce you. This note is legal tender. The performative Austin had found in a wedding and a ship's naming is made here the foundation of every institution a society has, and the paper in a wallet stays paper until the sentence printed across it is one an institution stands behind.
suggested_refs: John Searle, The Construction of Social Reality (Free Press, 1995)

stops.campa: Rationality in Action attacks the model of rational choice that economics and decision theory had settled on, in which an agent has fixed desires and reasons only about the means of satisfying them. Searle argues that the model leaves out the gap: the space between deliberating and acting in which a self decides, and in which a reason can be recognized as good and still not acted on. The book is published by MIT Press, his second with them in ten years.

Fifty-eight years after he came up on a Rhodes scholarship, the Oxford press prints his summing-up.

stops.name: Safety Harbor: the death on the gulf coast
stops.date_confidence: date, place and age attested (Wikipedia; Daily Nous, 28 September 2025; Leiter Reports; The Daily Californian obituary; APA In Memoriam). Coordinate contradiction recorded and resolved outside the pool: the three lenses carried three different Safety Harbor pins, 27.9906/-82.6987, 28.0186/-82.6954 and 28.0086/-82.6923, spread across about two and a half kilometres and none of them the town. Wikipedia gives Safety Harbor as 28.0050 N, 82.6950 W, and all three lenses are unified on that. No street address, hospital or cause of death is in any source consulted.
stops.campa: John Searle dies in Safety Harbor, on the Florida gulf coast, at ninety-three, six years after the university took his title and a continent away from the campus where he had taught since 1959. No Berkeley office, no students, no lecture hall. The philosopher who argued that a mind is something a biological organ does, and that no arrangement of symbols could ever be one, stops on the seventeenth of September, 2025. The date is carried by the philosophy blogs before any newspaper has it.

stops.name: Berkeley: the notices and the thread beneath them
stops.date_confidence: the Daily Nous and Leiter Reports notices are dated 28 September 2025; the APA In Memoriam and the Daily Californian obituary are dated only to September and October 2025. Attribution corrected: the sentence about numerous liaisons with students is not a reader comment but Brian Leiter's own parenthetical in the body of the memorial post, verified verbatim including the original's misspelling of liaisons. Jennifer Hudin disputed it in a comment dated 22 January 2026, saying a six-month investigation found no evidence and that the complainant was not a student; Leiter replied on 23 January 2026. That exchange postdates this stop by four months and is recorded here rather than given a stop of its own. Nothing in it is adjudicated.
stops.campa: The American Philosophical Association, Daily Nous and the Daily Californian publish within days of one another, and every notice carries both halves: the work that reshaped the philosophy of language and mind, and the finding that ended his standing at Berkeley. Underneath one of them the argument goes on about what he had been. The writer of that notice states in a parenthesis that there is no serious doubt he had numerous liaisons with students over many years; a colleague answers, months later, that the investigation found no evidence of it and that the complainant was not a student. He replies the next day.
stops.quote: Searle was a pugilistic philosopher, much more interested in winning than in truth.
stops.quote_source: Ned Block, quoted in 'In Memoriam: John Searle (1932-2025)', Leiter Reports, 28 September 2025

stops.name: Berkeley: the archive that was never gathered
stops.date_confidence: the absence of a dedicated Searle collection is attested by the pool's afterlife lens, working from UC Berkeley Library subject guides, Calisphere and the Internet Archive course recordings. The date is an ordering device marking the state of the record after his death, not an event; month and day are arbitrary within that.
stops.campa: There is no Searle archive. His papers are not gathered anywhere as a collection: the Bancroft Library holds general faculty material, Calisphere carries scattered photographs and recordings, and what survives in bulk is a set of course webcasts, whole semesters of Philosophy of Mind and Philosophy of Language, uploaded to the Internet Archive and watched by people who were never at Berkeley. The lectures arguing that no machine understands anything sit on a server as text and audio. No collection has been proposed.
